design_detail: Cross-sectional FDG-PET study of regional brain glucose metabolism in the same 15 people with methamphetamine dependence as Volkow et al. (2001a), abstinent at least 2 weeks, and 21 non-using controls (18 of them also in the DAT study). Region-of-interest analysis (10 composite regions plus global) and statistical parametric mapping.
can_establish: That this user group had higher whole-brain and parietal metabolism and lower relative thalamic and striatal metabolism than this control group at the time of scanning.
cannot_establish: That methamphetamine caused the differences (no pre-use scan; large differences in smoking and sex ratio between groups), what the higher metabolism means biologically (the gliosis interpretation is speculation, as the authors say), or any cognitive consequence (tests were given to users only).

sample.recruitment: Users from several drug rehabilitation centres in the Los Angeles area; controls by local advertisement (p. 384).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: DSM-IV methamphetamine dependence; average use at least 0.5 g/day, 5 days a week, for at least 2 years; at least 2 weeks' abstinence (urine-confirmed). Excluded: HIV seropositivity, comorbid psychiatric or neurological illness, abnormal screening tests, addiction to drugs other than methamphetamine or nicotine, head trauma with loss of consciousness over 30 minutes (p. 384).
sample.demographics: Users: 6 men, 9 women, age 32 (SD 7). Controls: 15 men, 6 women, age 31 (SD 8) (p. 384). Women 60% vs 28% (p. 386). Smokers 73% vs 24% (p. 387). Education not reported.
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-centre heavy users against advertisement-recruited controls; sex ratio and smoking differ markedly; the authors also expect users drank more alcohol and used more cannabis than controls (p. 387).

exposure.measurement: Self-reported history corroborated by physician evaluation; urine toxicology at entry and before scanning (p. 384).
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Inclusion thresholds only in this paper (p. 384); detailed use history is tabulated in the companion DAT paper (Volkow et al., 2001a, Table 1).
exposure.polysubstance: Dependence on other drugs except nicotine excluded; the authors state users probably consumed more alcohol and cannabis than controls (p. 387).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: 12 users tested 2 weeks to 5 months after last use, 3 users 11–35 months (p. 384). Outpatients; the authors note the reported time since last use cannot be confirmed with certainty (p. 387).

comparison.controls: 21 healthy volunteers by advertisement, no history of drug abuse or dependence (p. 384).
comparison.matching: Age similar; sex and smoking not matched; separate analyses by sex reported as consistent (p. 386).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No pre-use scan; no IQ or education reported in this paper.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Excluded for drug abuse; the authors acknowledge possible denial of drug use by controls and that HIV was not tested in controls (p. 387).

outcomes.instruments: FDG-PET (one 20-minute emission scan at rest, eyes open); 114 regions of interest combined into 10 composite regions and global metabolism; relative measures = region/global; SPM98 (p. 384).
outcomes.validity_norms: Neuropsychological battery (motor, attention, memory, mood, NART) given to users only; no group or normative comparison (pp. 384, 387).
outcomes.operationalization: Group differences in absolute and relative regional metabolism; within-user correlations with test scores, years and dose of use, and days since last use.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Partial: threshold p<0.01 for regional comparisons, justified as midway between 0.05 and Bonferroni (p. 384); SPM at p<0.005 uncorrected with a cluster-size threshold of 250 pixels (p. 384). The 14% global difference (p<0.05) is reported as significant although it does not meet the paper's own p<0.01 threshold.

analysis.effect_sizes: Global metabolism 38.4 (SD 8) vs 33.6 (SD 5) µmol/100 g/min, 14% higher in users, t=2.2, df=34, p<0.05 (p. 384). Parietal cortex 20% higher (t=2.9, df=34, p<0.01; Figure 2). Frontal, temporal, occipital cortex and hippocampus 11–12% higher at p<0.05, described as not significant under the p<0.01 threshold (p. 384). Relative to global: parietal 5% higher; thalamus 17%, caudate 12%, putamen 6% lower (pp. 384–385; Figure 3); caudate difference larger than putamen (group × region F=4.8, df=1,34, p<0.05) (p. 385). Three users abstinent at least 11 months: relative caudate metabolism 12% lower than controls (t=3.6, df=22, p<0.002) (p. 385). No metabolic measure correlated with days since last use; parietal relative metabolism correlated with Grooved Pegboard r=0.73 (df=14, p<0.003); whole-brain metabolism correlated with years of use r=−0.62 but not after covarying age (p. 385).
analysis.covariates: Age for one correlation; sex examined by stratification (p. 386); smoking not addressed analytically.
analysis.selective_reporting: Neuropsychological results are reported only as the correlations that reached significance.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Higher global and parietal and lower relative thalamic and striatal glucose metabolism in 15 abstinent users than in 21 controls who differed in sex ratio and smoking.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The discussion and summary state that methamphetamine at the doses people take causes or induces long-lasting changes in brain metabolism (pp. 386–387) and that the findings should alert clinicians to a possible higher risk of neurodegenerative disease (p. 387). The limitations paragraph on the same page concedes the smoking imbalance, likely heavier alcohol and cannabis use in users, uncertain abstinence dates, and that cognitive tests were done in users only, so group differences in cognition cannot be determined (p. 387). The causal wording is not supported by the design; the hypermetabolism-as-gliosis reading is offered as speculation (pp. 386–387).

timeline.event: DAT study in the same users
Follow-up in the same programme: thalamic relative metabolism partly recovered; striatal did not
Critical review: higher absolute metabolism here was not replicated by London et al. (2004), who found no difference in global metabolism; the paper reports no cognitive results and no education data

replication.where_it_stands: The direction of whole-brain metabolic differences is not consistent across groups (Hart et al., 2012, p. 597). Lower relative striatal metabolism in users is more consistent but shares the same confounding by smoking and selection.

funding.funder: US Department of Energy contract (Brookhaven National Laboratory); National Institute on Drug Abuse grants; Office of National Drug Control Policy; NIH General Clinical Research Center grant (p. 388).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Same group and sample as Volkow et al. (2001a).

what_would_settle_it: Longitudinal imaging from before regular use, or comparison groups matched on smoking, sex and other drug use, with cognition measured in both groups against norms.

domains.note: Smoking 73% vs 24%; women 60% vs 28%; probable alcohol and cannabis differences; none adjusted.
Abstinence duration self-reported in outpatients (acknowledged p. 387).
Different recruitment sources for the two groups.
FDG-PET objective; uncorrected SPM threshold; blinding not reported.
Global difference reported as significant despite missing the stated threshold; cognitive results reported only as significant correlations.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Metabolic group differences are measured objectively but are confounded by smoking and sex at a scale that could plausibly produce them, and the multiple-comparison rule is applied inconsistently.

key_findings.finding: Whole-brain glucose metabolism was 14% higher in 15 users than in 21 controls (38.4 vs 33.6 µmol/100 g/min, t=2.2, df=34, p<0.05), most in the parietal cortex (20%).
key_findings.note: p<0.05 does not meet the paper's own p<0.01 threshold for multiple comparisons.

key_findings.finding: Relative to whole-brain metabolism, users had lower metabolism in the thalamus (17%), caudate (12%) and putamen (6%), and higher in parietal cortex (5%).
Three users abstinent 11–35 months also had 12% lower relative caudate metabolism than controls.
No metabolic measure correlated with days since last use; thalamic and striatal metabolism did not correlate with any test score.
Smokers were 73% of users and 24% of controls; women 60% and 28%.
The authors state that neurocognitive tests were done only in users, so it cannot be determined how much the groups differed.

reporting_issues.issue: The 14% global metabolic difference (t=2.2, p<0.05) is presented as significant, but the methods set p<0.01 as the significance threshold for multiple comparisons, and other regions with similar t values (2.0–2.4) are described as not significant.
reporting_issues.consequence: The headline 'higher whole-brain metabolism' finding does not meet the paper's own criterion.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations in 15 users are reported with df=14 (expected 13).
